1:
The psalm carries a title that has baffled its interpreters, and the witnesses open by turning it over before they touch the first cry. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports the inscription — "To the chief Musician on Neginoth, upon Sheminith" — which the Chaldee renders "to be sung on neginoth, a harp of eight strings"; neginoth he takes for stringed instruments in general and sheminith for one of eight strings, though he grants that the variety of ancient and modern guesses shows that nothing certain is known of it. The reformed John Calvin is of the same mind, inclining to think the word points rather to the tune than to a harp, and adding drily that the Jews themselves have no sure knowledge of their ancient music. The latin-fathers Augustine had already read the obscure phrase "of the eighth" as a figure of the day of judgment — the world's seven thousand years passing as seven days and the eighth dawning as the age to come — yet he checks the speculation with the Lord's own word that it is not ours to know the times, so that no man should arrogate that day to himself by any reckoning of years.

Beneath the title all agree on the psalm's character. Clarke names it the first of the seven Penitential Psalms, supposing it written under some grievous disease that followed the sin with Bathsheba, so that it is the very language of a true penitent who sees, in Bishop Horne's words, "above, an angry God ... within, the gnawing worm." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe a sleepless, tearful night and three strophes climbing from a cry of distress to believing confidence; yet, because the psalm contains no confession of sin, they wonder whether the church has rightly numbered it among the penitential seven.

On the opening plea the witnesses converge, with one careful qualification. Gill notes that God rebukes his own people by his Spirit, his word, and his providences, but always in love and never in wrath, however much they fear otherwise. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry insists the prayer is not "rebuke me not" at all — for whom God loves he chastens — but "rebuke me not in thy anger, though I have deserved it"; the ache of the body is tolerable if only the heart be not made to ache by the sense of divine displeasure. Calvin hears the same submission: David owns the stroke as the just recompense of his sins, doubts that a bodily disease is even in view, and asks only that God not deal with him in strict justice. The puritan-evangelical C.H. Spurgeon adds that it were folly to pray against the golden hand that enriches by its blows — "Corn is cleaned with wind, and the soul with chastenings" — and begs only that the rod not become a sword. Ellicott alone strikes a different note: the sublime thought that pain is a discipline of love might be heard here, were it not that the context shows the sufferer praying for the chastisement to be altogether taken away, an echo, he observes, of Ps. 38:1.
2:
With the wrath deprecated, the psalmist turns to open petition, and the witnesses gather on the two cries "have mercy upon me ... for I am weak" and "heal me; for my bones are vexed." The reformed John Gill marks that David pleads no merit of his own and makes no mention of former righteousness, but throws himself wholly upon the mercy of God in Christ. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the same self-emptying and presses it further: "I have no merit; I deserve all I feel and all I fear"; no earthly physician can reach a malady in which body and soul are diseased together, and the word for "weak" he renders as an utter exhaustion of strength, the sufferer unable even to take his food, the disease having entered into the very bones.

The grammatical-historical witnesses sharpen the Hebrew. Charles Ellicott notes that "I am weak" properly means to wither or languish, like the drooping herb of Hos. 4:3 and the failing vine of Isa. 16:8, while "vexed" — so the Septuagint and Vulgate — is literally "affrighted," the shudder that Virgil pictures running cold through the bones. Keil and Delitzsch read the plea as founded on the sufferer's yearning still to praise God: he begs the Lord to turn to him again and to rescue his soul, in which the affliction has struck deep root, and to do it on the ground of his mercy toward sinners.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers over the strange spectacle of a stricken king. Though David was a king, he was sick and pained; his imperial crown could not keep his head from aching, for great men are men and subject to the common calamities of life; though a man of war from his youth, and though a good man, neither his strength nor his goodness could keep him in health. Henry hears in the groan the accent of the message concerning Lazarus — "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick" — and bids us take comfort that sickness and pain have been the lot of some of the best of the saints, who by their example teach us to spread our trouble before the God who is for the body and takes cognizance of its ailments. The witnesses do not divide; whether the vexing of the bones be read as the invasion of disease or as the trembling of terror, all agree that the prayer rests not on the sufferer's worth but on the mercy he flees to.
3:
"But thou, O LORD, how long?" — the broken question that trails off unfinished draws the witnesses to the meeting-place of grief and faith. The reformed John Gill first weighs the deeper wound of the verse, that not the bones only but "my soul is also sore vexed," exceedingly troubled and even terrified: by indwelling sin and actual transgression, by the hidings of God's face, by the temptations of Satan, and by the fear of death, to which the saints under the old covenant were especially liable. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the unfinished cry as the impatience of pain — "how long shall I continue under this malady? how long will it be before thou speak peace to my troubled heart?"

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds in the very brokenness of the sentence its power. The words halt, as they halt again in Ps. 90:13, and he calls the cry "belief in unbelief" — faith clinging where it cannot yet see. "Domine quousque," he recalls, was Calvin's own motto, and the story ran that the most intense grief could never wring from the Reformer another word than that. In its larger, national form this faith amid despair speaks in the angel's plea of Zech. 1:12 and the martyrs' cry of Rev. 6:10, the whole church learning to press the same unanswered question. The sentence is never filled out, its "how long" left hanging without an answer, and that very silence is, for Ellicott, the mark of a faith that dares to ask what it cannot yet resolve.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers up what completed the sufferer's misery — that his trouble was not only sharp but long, continued upon him a great while, which is just what the expostulation "how long?" lets slip. Henry weighs, too, how the vexation of the soul is much more grievous than the vexation of the bones, for the spirit of a man will sustain his bodily infirmity while it is itself in good plight, but a wounded spirit is a grief past bearing. And Henry draws the lesson the address itself teaches: at such a time it is to the living God that we must betake ourselves, who is the only physician both of body and mind, and not, like the faithless of old, to the Assyrians or to the god of Ekron. The witnesses do not divide. They hear in the half-sentence neither a settled complaint against God nor a lapse from faith, but the very accent of a soul that can no longer frame its trouble into words, yet still turns, with its "how long," to the only One who can end it.
4:
The cry "Return, O LORD" assumes a painful distance between the soul and its God, and the witnesses are careful how they speak of it. The reformed John Gill guards the doctrine first: God is immense and omnipresent, everywhere at once, so that going away and returning cannot properly be ascribed to him; yet he may be said to depart from his people as to sensible communion, when he hides his face and withdraws the comfortable influences of his love, and to return when he visits them again and manifests his favour. The going and the returning, then, are not changes in God but in the soul's sense of him: he stands where he stood, while the believer, for his sin, has lost the light of his face and now begs to have it restored. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the word the confession of a backslider: "Once I had the light of thy countenance; by sin I have forfeited this; I have provoked thee to depart: O Lord, return!" It is an awful thing, he owns, to be forced to say "Return," for the word supposes a departure; and yet what mercy that a backslider may return at all, and return in the expectation that God will return to him — the most humbling and the most hopeful word, at once, that a penitent can utter.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, fasten on the single Hebrew word for "return," whose accent is thrown forward onto the last syllable that it may not be swallowed up in pronunciation; God has turned away, and the whole prayer is that he would turn back, rescue the soul in which the affliction has struck root, and grant salvation on the ground of his mercy toward sinners.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the sum of the psalmist's desires — that God would receive him into favour again and be reconciled, "Return, O Lord, and show thyself nigh to me"; that he would especially preserve the inward man, delivering the soul from sinning, from sinking, from perishing for ever; and that he would do it all, as the last clause pleads, not for any worth of the sufferer but "for thy mercies' sake." It is among the best of all encouragements in prayer, Henry says, to plead the mercy of God; and the witnesses close in one accord, that the God who seemed to stand at a distance is entreated to draw near, and entreated on no ground but his own free compassion.
5:
The plea now shifts from the sufferer's need to God's own glory, and the witnesses read "in death there is no remembrance of thee" as an argument pressed upon heaven itself. The reformed John Gill takes it plainly: a dead man can make no mention of the goodness, truth, power, and faithfulness of God, nor of his works of nature or of grace, and is in this respect wholly useless to the living. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns it into a motive for the cure — man is made to glorify God on earth, an end the grave cannot serve; "heal my body, and heal my soul, that I may be rendered capable of loving and serving thee here below." John Wesley reads "remembrance" as the public celebration of God's grace in the land of the living, to the edification of the church, which is not the work of the other life.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the verse in its ancient frame, comparing the like plea of Ps. 30:9 and Isa. 38:18: the Israelite's natural dread of death was deepened by the thought that the grave cut him off from the privileges of the covenant. The word rendered "grave" is sheol, the underworld, in the early conception a vast sepulchral cave shut by gates of stone or iron, where all the dead lie side by side without sense of light or sound — something more than death and yet not life, the very sleep of death. Homer's shades keep some interest in the living world, but the Hebrew rephaim are weaker still, shadowy existences who know not anything; and it is just this undeveloped picture, Ellicott argues, that tells against assigning the psalm a late date.

The reformed John Calvin had heard David, in composing the psalm, regret that by being taken out of the world he would be robbed of the opportunity of praising God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the plea into two senses: in the second death there is no glad remembrance of God, for the lost only blaspheme him; and even the death of the body ends our service of his kingdom here below. The courtiers in the royal presence are most happy, Henry grants, but the soldiers in the field are more useful: "to depart and be with Christ is most happy for the saints themselves, but for them to abide in the flesh is more profitable for the church." So the witnesses gather to one plea: the psalmist asks his life not merely for his own sake but that he may go on giving God the thanks the grave would silence.
6:
The lament sinks to its lowest point in a chamber wet with tears, and the witnesses dwell on the nightlong grief of one "weary with my groaning." The reformed John Gill spreads out the many springs of that groaning — bodily illness, the guilt of actual sin, the hidings of God's face, the sense of divine wrath, the assaults of Satan, and the fear of death — and observes how the weariness is at last bodily as well as inward: the psalmist groaned until he was weary of his very groaning, for inward groaning tells upon the frame, wasting the animal spirits and consuming the flesh until faintness follows. He is weary, Gill allows, of his disease, or of his sin, or of both at once.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the poetry of the drenched couch, setting it beside the sleepless bed of Homer's Odyssey — "the couch for ever watered with my tears" — and remarks that the peoples of the East give free outward vent to a sorrow which the colder races of the West are trained to suppress or hide. The tears are not a weakness to be concealed but the native language of grief.

That very point the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses into a defence of the weeping king: it well becomes the greatest spirits to be tender and to relent under the tokens of God's displeasure; the David who could face Goliath himself melts into tears at the remembrance of sin, and it is no diminution at all to his character to do so. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same thread into a portrait of true penitence. Where the Pharisees disguised their faces that they might appear unto men to mourn, David mourned in the night upon the bed where he lay, no eye witnessing his grief but the eye of him who is all eye — as Peter, afterward, went out and wept bitterly. It has often been the lot of the best of men to be men of sorrows, Henry reminds us, our Lord Jesus himself among them, so that the way of the saints lies through a vale of tears to which we must accommodate ourselves. Sorrow for sin, Henry insists, ought to be great sorrow, and David's was so great that he watered his couch and made his bed to swim. The witnesses do not divide. They hear in the flooded bed no unmanly collapse but the honest overflow of a heart truly humbled, whose tears, shed in secret, are the fitting tribute of a penitent under the hand of God.
7:
Weeping so long together has at last told upon the very organ of weeping, and the witnesses read "mine eye is consumed because of grief" as the visible wearing-away of a wept-out man. The reformed John Gill notes that the word carries the sense of anger and the sorrow that rises from it, so that the grief may be indignation at his enemies who rejoice over him, or the felt weight of God's own displeasure; either way it vented itself in such floods of tears that the sight was hurt, for through much weeping the eye is weakened and grows dim. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders the Hebrew bluntly — the eye is "blasted, withered, sunk in my head."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott refines the picture. "Consumed" means sunken, literally fallen away, and it is the very word the Septuagint had used for "vexed" in the earlier plea, so that the same trouble which shook the bones now hollows the eye. Grief has stamped upon the sufferer the marks of premature age, as it did upon Job in Job 17:7 and the psalmist of Ps. 31:9; and Ellicott recalls Homer's word that mortals grow old quickly out of trouble.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fixes on the cause the verse itself names, that the eye waxed old "because of all mine enemies." David had more courage and consideration than to mourn thus for any outward affliction; it was when sin sat heavy upon his conscience and his soul was wounded with the sense of God's wrath and his withdrawings that he grieved and mourned in secret, till even his soul refused to be comforted, and in this great sorrow, Henry adds, he was a type of Christ, who often wept. Yet his enemies rejoiced in his sufferings and put bad constructions upon his tears, and the triumphs of wicked men in the sorrows of the saints add very much to their grief. So the closing clause binds together the two strands of the psalm — the inward wound of sin and displeasure, and the outward scorn of watching foes — into a single image of a face grown old before its time. The witnesses do not divide. Whether the grief that consumes the eye be indignation, or the sense of wrath, or the sting of mockery, all read the wasted eye as the body's confession of a soul worn down, and set it, as the psalm does, on the very threshold of the sudden turn to comfort that follows.
8:
"Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity" — and with that sudden command the whole temper of the psalm changes, the groaning man of the previous verses speaking now with the confidence of one already answered. The reformed John Gill marks the swiftness of it, a quick passage from an uncomfortable frame to a comfortable one; the "workers of iniquity" he takes for the psalmist's open enemies, or else the secret, hypocritical courtiers who wished him dead, and he reflects that it is the lot of God's people to dwell among such — Lot in Sodom, David in Meshech and the tents of Kedar, the lily among the thorns.

The puritan-evangelical voices dwell longest here. Matthew Henry reads the dismissal as the act of a man newly assured that his lot is among the chosen and not among the sinners whose portion he had feared to share; the enemies who taunted him with "Where is thy God?" and tempted him to fling away his religion are now sent packing, and, as a king, David renews his purpose to be a terror to evildoers — words our Lord himself would borrow at Luke 13:27. Henry hears the ground of the confidence in the twice-repeated "the Lord hath heard": while the psalmist is yet speaking he is aware that God hears, as in Isa. 65:24, and so speaks of it as a thing already done; his tears had a loud voice in the ears of the God of mercy, for "silent tears are not speechless ones." C.H. Spurgeon takes up the same wonder: after a night of weeping joy comes in the morning, and the pardoned man rises to sweep his house of the wicked, for a soul that has found peace will hate the sins that cost the Saviour his blood. Is there a voice in weeping? Spurgeon asks; and answers that weeping is the eloquence of sorrow, an unstammering orator understood in every tongue on earth and in heaven.

Adam Clarke and John Wesley confirm the reading from their own wesleyan-arminian quarter: the enemies had upbraided the sufferer with his transgressions to cast him into despair, but the Lord had pitifully beheld his sorrows and mercifully forgiven his sins; it was by the workings of God's grace upon his heart that David knew his prayer accepted, his very tears being cries to God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls it the morning of revived faith after the night of sorrow, when the psalmist can at last turn to his maligners in the certainty that the prayer he had poured, as he feared, into deaf and unsympathising ears has in truth been heard. Keil and Delitzsch note how, even before the plaint is ended, the divine light breaks in: thrice over his confidence flashes out, the plain "hath heard" stating the fact and the assurance of acceptance drawing its consequence. The witnesses stand together: the rout of the enemy begins the moment the soul is sure it has been heard.
9:
What the previous verse announced in the heat of triumph this verse repeats in a calmer certainty, and the witnesses attend to the quiet doubling of the assurance, "the LORD hath heard my supplication; the LORD will receive my prayer." The reformed John Gill reads the "supplication" as the very sum of all that the psalmist had poured out from the opening cry onward — the deprecating of God's anger and hot displeasure, the plea for grace and mercy, the longing for healing of soul or body, for the return of God's presence, and for deliverance out of every trouble and from death itself. The word, he notes, properly signifies petitions for grace and mercy, such as are made under the influence of the Spirit of grace and of supplication; and it was these, offered in that Spirit, that God had heard, so that the assurance rests not on the worth of the asking but on the grace that prompted it. These were no cold formalities, Gill implies, but the earnest pourings-out of a soul in trouble, and it is such prayer that God is never deaf to.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, hear the weight of the two tenses set side by side: the first verb states the accomplished fact — the Lord has heard the loud sobbing that rose toward heaven — and the second draws out its consequence, that he will therefore accept and take up the prayer; the confidence of the answered past becomes the ground of the assured future.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry knits the two clauses into a single argument of faith: "he has heard the voice of my supplication, and therefore he will receive my prayer; for he gives, and does not upbraid with former grants." The God who has already answered will not turn away the petition still upon the lips, for it is not his way to reproach a suppliant with the mercies of the past. By the very workings of that grace upon his heart, Henry observes, David knew his prayer was graciously accepted, and so did not doubt that it would in due time be effectually answered; and from the gracious hearing of this one cry he may safely infer the like favourable audience of all his other prayers. The witnesses do not divide. They hear in the twice-named "the LORD" the settled peace of a soul that has passed from asking into assurance, and that reckons the prayer already received in heaven though the full answer be not yet seen on earth.
10:
The psalm ends by turning upon the enemies, and here the witnesses genuinely divide over whether the closing words are a sentence of doom or a prayer for their rescue. The reformed John Gill holds the verse open: the clause may be read as a prophecy — "they shall be ashamed" — of what will surely come; or, if taken as an imprecation, it wishes them no real ill, for it would be well indeed if the wicked, who are not ashamed of their abominations now, were brought to a true and shame-faced repentance, and if they are not ashamed in this life they will be hereafter, when the Judge of quick and dead appears. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the hopeful reading hard. Adam Clarke prays outright, "may they as deeply deplore their transgressions as I have done mine; may they return; may they be suddenly converted" — the original, he insists, will bear this sense, and it is the most congenial to Christian principles. John Wesley reads the same way: let them be ashamed of their vain confidence, and "return" — that is, repent of their sins and come back to their obedience.

Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears not conversion but rout. The verbs are better rendered as present or future, the psalmist seeing with the eye of faith the answer already granted; and "return" means to retire discomfited and in failure, as Milton turned the verse — the foes struck blank with confusion, growing red with shame, and hasting back the way they came. On this reading the answer to the prayer is not the sinner's repentance but the enemy's overthrow, the rout that faith already sees accomplished. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds both readings together without forcing a choice: the words may be a prayer that the enemies be vexed at themselves in penitence and returned to a better mind, or, if they will not be converted, a prediction of their confusion and ruin — for the evil they wished returns upon their own heads. They had rejoiced that David was sore vexed in v.3, and now they shall be sore vexed themselves; those who will not give glory to God shall have their faces filled with everlasting shame. So the psalm that opened in the terror of divine anger closes in the calm of divine acceptance, and its last word over the enemies is left, deliberately, between a threat and a plea — ruin if they persist, but mercy still open if they will be ashamed and turn.
